replacement.objective: Read possession quality before leaving a defensive support position.
replacement.briefing: D1 is beside a bouncing loose puck. Gold 1 is close enough to contest the next touch. YOU are the other defender near the front of your net; possession is not established. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The puck has no owner in this setup, matching the stated contested touch.

questions.prompt: Is the puck currently assigned to either team?
questions.explanation: The puck has no owner in this setup, matching the stated contested touch.

questions.prompt: Choose two reasons to avoid leaving too early.

options.text: Every loose puck will become a breakout

questions.explanation: Possession and remaining threats matter. A partner’s proximity is not proof of control.

questions.prompt: Arrange a cautious support read.

options.text: Check the remaining threat near the net
Move to support the outcome you actually see

questions.explanation: Checks can overlap; the important point is not assuming a win.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to balance net-side support with a possible outlet angle.
questions.explanation: The example changes the outlet angle while remaining closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2. Recheck both opponents; location alone does not establish coverage.

questions.prompt: D1 now controls the puck and Gold 1 skates past. What can you reassess?

options.text: Whether a loose-puck battle still exists unchanged
Whether Gold 2 has disappeared from the play
Whether to widen into a clear outlet

questions.explanation: Secure control may permit a wider support position, but Gold 2 still needs to be read.

questions.prompt: What visible sign would tell you this situation has become a breakout opportunity?
questions.explanation: Describe controlled possession and a usable next option, rather than simply seeing D1 near the puck.

questions.prompt: What remains unknown at this freeze?

options.text: Which team will control the bouncing puck

questions.explanation: The puck has no owner, so possession is unresolved; if D1 controls it, YOU support breakout, while Gold control starts a defensive read.

questions.prompt: Which two cues should YOU communicate to D1?

options.text: Gold 1 is close to the next touch
The net-side support lane is covered or open
Tell D1 the puck is theirs before the contest is settled

questions.explanation: Pressure distance and inside support tell D1 whether to protect or move it; the bounce direction is not guaranteed.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the middle while staying closer to Navy’s net than Gold 2.
questions.explanation: The example is nearer the middle and still closer to the defended net than Gold 2. The net is not between YOU and Gold 1. If gold gains control, reassess pressure and coverage before moving again.

questions.prompt: What visible sign would change your job from partner support to breakout support?
questions.explanation: Clear control on D1’s stick changes the task from contest coverage to outlet and spacing; if the puck remains loose, keep the net-side lane protected.

options.text: A rush directly to the far net

options.text: A position closer to Navy’s net

options.text: Notice F1’s position farther up ice

questions.prompt: Why can two forwards at similar depth make D1’s options easier to defend?

questions.prompt: What could YOU call before moving closer to Navy’s net than F1?

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than F1 and toward the middle.

questions.prompt: When might different depths give D1 more options?
questions.explanation: Different depths can create distinct passing angles if both remain reachable. One defender does not automatically cover both players at the same depth, and staggering does not guarantee an open route.

questions.prompt: Pick two useful checks for your next support movement.

options.text: The angle for a return pass
Whether remaining level with D2 looks tidy

options.text: Offer support closer to Navy’s net than D2
Present an option and read the next pass

questions.explanation: These are suggested actions; do not delay necessary defensive support merely to finish a pattern.

Remain closer to Navy’s net than the old puck position indefinitely
Follow Gold 1 away from the developing play

options.text: I will offer a return option closer to our net
I will stand on D2’s lane

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 angles toward the boards, choose a deeper return target to reassess.
questions.explanation: The example changes the return angle and depth. It does not guarantee a clear lane after Gold 1 moves; check pressure and reach before calling for the pass.

questions.prompt: How can communicating a planned return angle help D2?
questions.explanation: A clear call can help D2 locate the intended option. Confirm readiness and lane access rather than assuming the call makes it available.

questions.prompt: Which side is F1 using for the entry?

options.text: The wide lane near the boards

questions.explanation: F1 carries in a wide lane near the side boards.

questions.prompt: Which two details matter before taking the suggested middle route?

options.text: Whether every entry requires the same net drive

questions.explanation: The middle route is a teaching option under these conditions, not a mandatory route on every entry.

questions.prompt: Arrange a support read for the wide entry.

options.text: Move on a different useful route

questions.explanation: The supporter must continue checking for changing coverage.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to illustrate a separate middle support route.
questions.explanation: This creates a different lane from F1. Actual route timing and the defender’s movement must still be judged.

questions.prompt: If Gold 2 steps into that middle route, what could YOU change?

options.text: Continue through Gold 2 because the drill named a route
Delay or choose another support lane

questions.explanation: A defender closing a route changes the available options; another route may be equally useful.

questions.prompt: Why should F1 and the supporting forward avoid filling exactly the same lane?
questions.explanation: Different lanes can ask defenders to cover more space, provided the support remains reachable and onside.

questions.prompt: Which space should YOU offer to complement F1’s wide entry?

options.text: The controlled middle route toward the far-post area
The same wide lane beside F1

questions.explanation: The middle route complements F1’s wide lane and gives the carrier a different angle toward the far post; if Gold 2 closes it, keep separation and find the next visible lane.

questions.prompt: Which two checks should precede a middle route?

options.text: Whether the far-post route is automatically clear because F1 is wide

questions.explanation: The defender’s inside position and carrier control determine whether the middle route helps; F1 being wide does not by itself mean the far-post route is clear too.

questions.prompt: Move YOU nearer the middle as an early support step, without overtaking F1.
questions.explanation: The example moves YOU toward the middle while remaining closer to Navy’s net than F1. It is an early support point, not a position at the far post. Recheck both defenders before continuing.

questions.prompt: Why does the far-post route help more than simply avoiding F1’s lane?
questions.explanation: A route toward the far-post area may provide another scoring angle if it is reachable and unblocked. It is one option; keeping separation elsewhere can also be useful depending on coverage.

questions.prompt: What has F1 explicitly done before this freeze?
questions.explanation: The briefing states a delay and the puck remains assigned to F1.

questions.prompt: Which two reads help you stay available?

options.text: The assumption that maximum speed always helps

questions.explanation: Arrival timing can matter more than simply skating past the puck.

questions.prompt: Order a suggested response to F1’s delay.

options.text: Adjust arrival to remain an option

questions.explanation: Scanning and timing can overlap; this is a routine rather than a compulsory sequence.

questions.prompt: Move YOU into an example delayed support pocket.
questions.explanation: A pocket inside and behind F1 may provide an option without overrunning the puck. Defender reach is not validated here.

questions.prompt: F1 loses control while delaying. What must you reassess first?

options.text: How to arrive even farther ahead of the puck
Whether the team now needs defensive support
Which attacking route to continue automatically

questions.explanation: Possession loss may change the job before the planned support pass can happen.

questions.prompt: What does “saving ice” mean in this particular scene?
questions.explanation: Explain remaining in reachable space at the right time, not simply standing still or refusing to attack.

questions.prompt: What useful call can YOU make while F1 protects the puck?

options.text: I am looking for support space behind your route

questions.explanation: Communicate the intended support and call availability only after checking the lane. F1 does not have to pass immediately.

questions.prompt: Which two cues decide whether YOU should arrive now?

options.text: Whether F1 slowing means the support route must stay fixed

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a staggered support pocket behind F1’s lane.

questions.prompt: What does saving ice mean here, and when would it stop helping?
questions.explanation: It means arriving connected without crowding F1, preserving a route while the puck is protected; if the route becomes covered or F1 loses control, reassess.
